Git 2.50.1: every command was run in the lab

toc.title: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository
What a commit is: snapshots and objects
Branches, HEAD and the history graph

html:
1Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository

Every Git command moves content between three areas. The figure shows them, and the table names what each one holds.

Area What it holds Where it lives What moves content in
Working tree The files you see and edit Your project folder Your editor
Staging area (index) The proposed next snapshot .git/index git add
Repository Every commit ever made .git/objects git commit

git add copies the current content of a file into the staging area. git commit turns the staging area into a new commit. Because staging is a separate step, you choose which changes go into a commit.

So one file can exist in three versions at once. git show HEAD:cart.txt reads the repository, git show :cart.txt reads the staging area (the colon means the index), and cat reads the working tree. The short status MM means a staged change plus a newer unstaged one.

echo "cart: 2 items" > cart.txt
git add cart.txt
echo "cart: 3 items" > cart.txt
git status -s
git show HEAD:cart.txt
git show :cart.txt
cat cart.txt

MM cart.txt
cart: empty
cart: 2 items
cart: 3 items
Tip

. A commit contains what is staged, not what is in your folder. If you edit a file after git add, add it again, or the newer edit stays out of the commit.

2What a commit is: snapshots and objects

A commit is a snapshot of the whole project at one moment, plus a message, an author, a committer with a time, and its parent commit. Git does not store diffs; it computes them by comparing two snapshots. A file that did not change is not copied again: the new snapshot points at the same stored content.

The first commit has no parent. A merge commit has two (module 4). Following the parents from any commit gives the history.

Git stores everything as objects of four types.

Type What it stores
blob The content of one file, without its name
tree One folder: names, modes, and the blobs or trees inside
commit A tree, the parents, author, committer and message
tag An annotated tag: a name, a message and the object it marks

git cat-file -t prints the type of an object and git cat-file -p prints its content. Your hashes will differ from the ones below.

git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD

commit
tree 362d57bb8c31f3a23f49169d24897baacb3c69de
parent b7d7b3c567f8262169bcee84bcec6143f8945278
author Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1794884992 +0500
committer Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1794884992 +0500

Update cart

The commit holds one tree. The tree lists each file as a blob with mode 100644, and each subfolder as another tree with mode 040000. git ls-files --stage shows the same list for the staging area: mode, blob hash, a stage number of 0, and the path.

git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}
git ls-files --stage
git cat-file -t HEAD:README.md

100644 blob 59b51e2b4c05ada748d0ef8d5856c687ffe1a7cb	README.md
100644 blob a51cf18012d71630f15e7ed7ca09c689351a7ef2	cart.txt
100644 59b51e2b4c05ada748d0ef8d5856c687ffe1a7cb 0	README.md
100644 a51cf18012d71630f15e7ed7ca09c689351a7ef2 0	cart.txt
blob
Tip

. Use git cat-file -p to look at any object. Nothing in Git is hidden once you know a hash, and reading never changes anything.

An annotated tag is a fourth object type with its own message. A lightweight tag is only a name that points at a commit, so its type is commit (module 3).

3Hashes: names made from content

Every object has a hash: 40 hexadecimal characters computed from its content. The same content always gives the same hash. Two files with identical content share one blob, and an unchanged file keeps its blob in the next snapshot. git hash-object README.md computes the blob hash of a file.

A commit hash covers the tree, the parents, the author and the message. Change any of them, as git commit --amend does, and you get a new hash.

A short hash is the first seven characters by default. Git accepts any prefix that is unambiguous, and git log --oneline prints short hashes. Loose objects are stored in .git/objects, in a folder named after the first two characters.

Name What it means
HEAD The commit you are on
HEAD~1 or HEAD^ Its parent
main The commit at the tip of that branch
v1.0 The commit a tag marks
a1b2c3d A commit, by short hash

git rev-parse turns any of these names into a full hash, and --short gives the short form.

4Branches, HEAD and the history graph

A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. It is a small file in .git/refs/heads that holds one hash. When you commit, Git moves the pointer of the current branch to the new commit. Creating a branch only writes another small file, so it is instant and costs almost nothing.

HEAD says which branch you are on. The file .git/HEAD holds ref: refs/heads/main. Switching branches rewrites that file and the files in your folder. Branches do not contain commits; they point at them, and each commit points at its parent.

cat .git/HEAD
cat .git/refs/heads/main
git rev-parse --short main
git branch feature
git switch feature
cat .git/HEAD

ref: refs/heads/main
d92e6f47ebfe13e5f621139a3144bbee3f44c470
d92e6f4
Switched to branch 'feature'
ref: refs/heads/feature

A new branch points at the same commit as the branch you made it from. After one commit on feature, main has not moved, and the new commit's parent is the old tip.

HEAD can also hold a raw hash instead of a branch name. That is a detached HEAD (module 3). After housekeeping, Git may move a branch into .git/packed-refs, but git rev-parse still finds it.

Tip

. Look inside .git to understand, but never edit it by hand. Ask Git with git rev-parse and git symbolic-ref HEAD instead.

Tip

. Think of a branch as a sticky note on a commit. Moving the note does not delete commits, and commits with no note on them can be lost.

5Practice Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Ada runs git add cart.txt, then edits cart.txt again and runs git commit -m "Update cart" without a second add. What does the new commit contain?

  • AThe newer edit, because commit always reads the working tree
  • BBoth versions of the file, stored one after the other in a commit
  • CThe staged version, because a commit records the staging area
  • DNothing, because Git refuses to commit a file edited after add
Show the answer

Answer: C. A commit is built from the staging area, so the later edit stays unstaged until it is added.

S2git status -s prints MM cart.txt. What does this tell Bob about the file?

  • AIt has two merge conflicts that he must resolve before committing
  • BIt was changed twice and both changes are already committed
  • CIt is tracked twice, once on each of two different branches
  • DIt has a staged change and a newer change that is not staged
Show the answer

Answer: D. The first M is the staging area against the last commit, and the second M is the working tree against the staging area.

S3cat .git/HEAD prints ref: refs/heads/feature. Cy now makes a commit. Which pointer moves?

  • AThe feature branch moves to the new commit
  • BThe main branch moves to the new commit
  • CHEAD moves to the first parent of the commit
  • DThe tag with the same name moves to the commit
Show the answer

Answer: A. HEAD names the current branch, and a commit moves that branch forward.

S4Bob runs git cat-file -t HEAD:README.md. What does it print, and why?

  • Atree, because every file lives inside a tree of its folder
  • Bcommit, because the file is read at the commit named HEAD
  • Ctag, because the colon marks the name of a tag object
  • Dblob, because it is the content of a single file only
Show the answer

Answer: D. A blob stores the content of one file without its name, and the name lives in the tree.

S5Ada copies README.md to README2.md and stages both files. How many blobs does Git need for the two files?

  • ATwo, because every path always gets its own object
  • BOne, because the hash comes from the content alone
  • CThree, because the tree needs a blob of its own too
  • DZero, because staged files are only stored at commit time
Show the answer

Answer: B. Identical content gives an identical hash, so both paths point to the same blob.

S6Cy runs git branch feature while on main and nothing else. What did Git create?

  • AA copy of every file in the project in a new folder
  • BA new commit with the same message as the last one
  • CA small file that holds the hash of the current commit
  • DA second repository inside .git for the new branch
Show the answer

Answer: C. A branch is a pointer, so creating one writes a file with a hash and copies nothing.

5.2 Recall questions

R1Name the three areas of Git.

Show the answer

The working tree, the staging area (index) and the repository.

R2Which four object types does Git store?

Show the answer

Blob, tree, commit and tag.

R3What does .git/HEAD hold while you are on main?

Show the answer

ref: refs/heads/main.

R4Which command turns a name such as HEAD or main into a full hash?

Show the answer

git rev-parse.

R5How many characters does a default short hash have?

Show the answer

Seven.

R6How many parents does the first commit of a repository have?

Show the answer

None.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Three areas Working tree, staging area (.git/index), repository (.git/objects)
Staging git add fills the index; a commit records the index, not the folder
Commit Snapshot plus message, author, committer and parent
Objects blob (file content), tree (folder), commit, tag; git cat-file -t and -p
Index listing git ls-files --stage shows mode, blob hash, stage 0, path
Hashes 40 hex characters from the content; short hash is seven; git rev-parse
Branch A file in .git/refs/heads holding one commit hash
HEAD .git/HEAD holds ref: refs/heads/main; commits move the current branch
